entry.title: A South African paper reframes early-warning analytics as strengths-based "early success indicators" (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A 2026 conceptual article in the Journal of Student Affairs in Africa, written by two student affairs staff members at the University of Pretoria, proposes 'early success indicators' as a strengths-based alternative to the deficit-oriented language of early warning or early alert systems, at an unnamed South African research-intensive university. Drawing on Siemens' Learning Analytics Model and student development theory, the authors map data points and institutional support mechanisms across the student lifecycle, from pre-registration to final assessments, grounded in the insights of academic success coaches, institutional leaders and data scientists. They argue that institutional collaboration, a culture of data transparency and timely, targeted advising matter as much as the predictive model itself.

Why it matters here: This is a direct conceptual caution from South Africa for PASS: it argues that framing predictive analytics around deficit language such as 'at risk' can itself undermine student success work, and that the data points and advising structures around a model matter as much as its accuracy, a reminder for PASS as it moves from the Wits School of Education's anonymised data towards advising interventions with Business Intelligence Services.

Majozi, P. C., & Mathabathe, K. C. (2026). Journal of Student Affairs in Africa. · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A stacking ensemble reaches 98 percent accuracy predicting graduation versus dropout in Indonesia (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Using 4,424 student records (34 predictors) from a public dataset, researchers built HLR-STACK, a stacking ensemble with a logistic-regression meta-learner over tree-based and boosting base learners, with in-fold SMOTE for class balancing and stratified 7-fold cross-validation. On the binary graduate-versus-dropout task (3,630 records) it reached 0.981 accuracy, and 0.844 accuracy on the three-class task (graduate, dropout, enrolled).

Why it matters here: Gives PASS a concrete, interpretable ensemble technique, combining a logistic-regression meta-learner with boosted base learners and SMOTE for class imbalance, that the team could trial on the Wits School of Education data, which likely has a similar imbalance between at-risk and on-track students.

Wijiyanto, Marjuni, A., Fanani, A. Z., & Basuki, R. S. (2026). · Peer-reviewed journal article, Ingénierie des Systèmes d'Information (IIETA)

entry.title: Turkish university opens three Erasmus+ doctoral mobility places to Azerbaijan, Georgia and Bangladesh (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Erzurum Technical University in Turkey opened applications on 22 April 2026, closing 15 May 2026, for three doctoral-level mobility places for one semester in the 2026 to 2027 academic year under its Erasmus+ KA171-HED project 2025-1-TR01-KA171-HED-000326726, one place each at Azerbaijan Technical University, Georgian Technical University and the Asian University for Women in Bangladesh. Selection combines GPA and a language test score, and grants include a monthly 700 euro stipend plus travel support, with a zero-grant option for students who forgo funding.

Why it matters here: This shows KA171 doctoral mobility working as a small, clearly resourced exchange between a non-European sending university and partner institutions on three continents, a practical template for how the Aix-Marseille/Wits project can structure its own doctoral places and funding rules between Europe and the Global South.

Erzurum Technical University. (2026, April 22). · University institutional announcement

entry.title: Educational service quality shapes Erasmus+ students' intentions to migrate, Turkish study finds (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A 2026 study in the Journal of Multidisciplinary Academic Tourism surveyed 127 undergraduate students who had taken part in Erasmus+ at a Turkish university and used structural equation modelling to test whether their rating of their home institution's service quality shaped their attitude to brain drain, that is, their inclination to migrate abroad. It found a positive, significant effect (beta = 0.40, p < 0.001): students who rated their education more highly were more inclined towards brain drain attitudes. The authors describe the study as one of the first to test this link empirically in an Erasmus+ setting.

Why it matters here: This is a direct empirical caution for the Aix-Marseille/Wits KA171 partnership: it suggests that raising the quality of mobility experiences can, on its own, strengthen rather than weaken Global South students' pull towards emigration, so the project's evaluation should track graduates' return and retention alongside satisfaction.

Ergün, B., Zorlu, Ö., & Aytekin, E. (2026). Journal of Multidisciplinary Academic Tourism. · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Survey of 136 engineering students finds high acceptance of a mobile gamified learning tool in an electrical machinery course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universitas Negeri Padang in Indonesia, with co-authors from Beirut Arab University and the University of Naples Parthenope, surveyed 136 Industrial Electrical Engineering students on their acceptance of MoGaLearn, a mobile-based gamified learning tool used in the electrical machinery course. Using the technology acceptance model and variance-based structural equation modelling, the study found perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, attitude and behavioural intention all had a significant positive influence on students' actual use of the tool, and that students showed a high overall level of acceptance.

Why it matters here: This gives the Wits CheMet project a validated instrument, the technology acceptance model, for measuring whether engineering students actually take up a gamified or digital assessment tool rather than just enjoying it, and a comparable sample size of 136 students to benchmark against its own surveys.

Candra, O., Yanto, D. T. P., Zaswita, H., Samala, A. D., Rawas, S., & Arcelus-Ulibarrena, J. M. (2026). International Journal of Online and Biomedical Engineering (iJOE). · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article (iJOE), CC-BY

entry.title: University of Granada joins Erasmus+ project on ethical AI for language teacher training (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The University of Granada announced on 16 December 2025 that it is a partner in the Erasmus+ KA220 project 'New-Gen Language Teachers: Empowering Language Teaching with Ethical AI-Enhanced Guidance', led by the University of Latvia with partners in Türkiye and Austria, running two years on a budget of 250,000 euros. Planned outputs include a 20-hour curriculum module on ethical AI use in language teaching, a game-based toolkit, an open-access multilingual MOOC, and piloting with 200 prospective English teachers before adaptation for undergraduate and postgraduate programmes.

Why it matters here: The project's ethical-AI curriculum module, toolkit and MOOC for training future language teachers are concrete, transferable materials the Aix-Marseille/Wits bilingual teacher education strand could trial or adapt, since both partnerships share the aim of using AI responsibly to prepare multilingual teachers.

University of Granada. (2025, December 16). · University institutional news page

entry.title: AI-based learning analytics correlate with student retention at a Lima institution (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A non-experimental, correlational study using documentary analysis of institutional data and student surveys found a high positive correlation (rho = 0.789, p < 0.05) between AI-based learning analytics and student retention at a Lima institution. The abstract reports that more than 98 percent of surveyed students showed medium or high levels of retention, with most students around 25 years old taking an average of seven courses.

Why it matters here: Gives PASS independent, peer-reviewed evidence from Latin America that AI-based analytics track meaningfully with retention, a correlational design the Wits/Emory team's own predictive-validation work could sharpen with causal or longitudinal methods.

Aguilar-David, I., Ricra-Mayorca, J. M., & Romero-Flores, L. A. (2025). LACCEI. · Peer-reviewed conference paper, LACCEI proceedings

entry.title: Escape room turns pre-exam review into a materials science game at Universitat Jaume I (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Academics at Universitat Jaume I report running an escape room with second-year Industrial Technologies Engineering students as a pre-exam review session in a Materials Science and Technology course, presented at EDULEARN25 in Palma (30 June to 2 July 2025). Students worked through crossword puzzles and short problems on mechanical properties and phase diagrams before earning an exercise from a previous final exam to solve together. A post-intervention questionnaire found higher motivation and engagement than in a traditional lecture, and practical assessment scores improved.

Why it matters here: The escape room is built directly on phase diagrams and mechanical properties, the same ground the Wits CheMet study wants gamified assessment to cover, and shows a low-cost, replicable exam-review format the project could trial alongside its own board and digital games.

Romero-Gavilán, F., & García-Cañadas, J. (2025). EDULEARN25 Proceedings. · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings paper (EDULEARN25)

entry.title: Northwestern's Structural Metallic Materials Group builds browser games on freeze-casting and additive manufacturing (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Northwestern Engineering reports, in an article published on 25 July 2023, that Professor David Dunand's Structural Metallic Materials Group has built browser games to teach materials science concepts: L.U.M.P.I Space Adventure and TetrIce, both based on freeze-casting (ice-templating) and porosity, and 3D Think, a puzzle matching 3D microstructure models to their cross-sections for additive manufacturing and tomography. TetrIce and 3D Think were built mainly by undergraduate computer science student Isaac Brown; the article reports no formal learning-outcome testing beyond playtesting feedback and a 2018 Serious Play Conference bronze medal for L.U.M.P.I.

Why it matters here: These games show how a university materials group turns specific microstructure concepts, porosity and freeze-casting here, into short browser games built partly by undergraduates; the same approach could produce quick digital add-ons for the crystallography and phase-transformation topics central to the Wits CheMet study, and the article is honest that formal evidence of learning gains is still missing, a gap this project's own assessment work could fill.

Mohney, M. (2023). Northwestern Engineering. · University institutional news article

entry.title: Think tank sets out the scale and visa barriers of labour and education migration from Africa to Germany (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Published on 2 July 2026 by Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, the brief reports that German employment visa applications from African countries rose from about 7,860 in 2019 to 29,415 in 2025, and vocational training and further education visa applications rose from 1,318 to 7,531 over the same period. It states that Ghana's study visa applications rose from 621 in 2019 to 1,340 in 2025, with 2,918 Ghanaian nationals enrolled at German universities in winter 2024/25, while Cameroonian nationals in German vocational training rose from 950 in 2019 to 5,260 by May 2026. The brief says available evidence suggests visa rejection rates for African applicants are significantly higher than for other regions of origin, though it gives no exact figures.

Why it matters here: This independent policy analysis offers a cautionary benchmark on visa friction and uneven access for African students and trainees moving to Europe, a reminder for the Wits-Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ exchange to monitor visa processing and equity of access for Wits participants travelling to France.

Kipp, D., Landmesser, E. & Heidland, T. (2026). SWP Megatrends Afrika Spotlight 75. · Think tank policy brief (Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik)

entry.title: Vocational teacher students complete a blended Erasmus+ exchange on artificial intelligence and education in the Netherlands (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Vocational teacher students from TAMK in Finland and partner institutions including ATU in Ireland took part in a Blended Intensive Programme called AI & Education, which combined online sessions on AI literacy starting in mid-February 2026 with a week-long in-person exchange at Hanze University of Applied Sciences in Groningen, Netherlands, from 23 to 27 March 2026. Teams created 12 AI-literacy exhibits in total, presented at an Interactive Pop-up AI Literacy Exhibition on 26 March 2026 held alongside Hanze's Digital Literacy Week. The student authors reported gains in technical skills, a more responsible and human-centred understanding of AI in teaching, and new international networks.

Why it matters here: This case gives a concrete, recent model of a short blended mobility format, combining virtual AI-literacy training with a brief in-person exchange, that the Wits-Aix-Marseille project could adapt for staff or master's students in bilingual teaching without requiring a full semester abroad, matching the project's interest in virtual and blended mobility with AI-supported teaching tools.

Acharya, B. & Korpua, H. (2026). TAOK-blogi, Tampere University of Applied Sciences. · University blog, first-person student account

entry.title: Turkish university's international relations office visits University of Dar es Salaam under KA171 staff training mobility (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Published on 12 February 2026, the article reports that the Directorate of International Relations of Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakıf University visited the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania as part of the KA171 Staff Training Mobility Programme. The visit involved discussions on internationalisation in higher education focused on the African and Tanzanian context, covering institutional opportunities, inclusiveness, gender responsiveness, sustainability and core European values. The article states the visit contributed to strengthening institutional collaboration and mutual understanding and supports the University of Dar es Salaam's internationalisation objectives and partnerships across the African region.

Why it matters here: This case shows how Erasmus+ KA171 staff mobility is already used specifically for the administrative and international relations staff who run exchange links between a European and an African university, directly matching the administrative staff mobility strand of the Wits-Aix-Marseille project.

Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakıf University (2026) · University institutional news report

entry.title: NTU's EARLI project flags students needing support before each new semester (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Nanyang Technological University's Education Transformation Office describes EARLI (Early AleRt for Learning Intervention), a fully automated pipeline that combines four models, a support vector machine, logistic regression, an LSTM network and a short-term gated LSTM, on historical performance data to flag incoming second and third year students across five STEM schools who most need academic support before each new semester. Predictions update and are validated every six months before a dashboard releases the flagged list to student care managers, who then contact students; the page reports a true positive rate of more than 70 percent among surveyed schools, and one school reported that most reached students saw their semester and cumulative GPA rise in the following academic year.

Why it matters here: EARLI is an operating example, not just a model, of exactly the loop PASS wants to build: a predictive flag feeding into a human advising workflow with a measured true positive rate, which PASS and the University's Business Intelligence Services could study as a template for turning Wits School of Education predictions into actual outreach. Its reliance on four combined classifiers, and its six monthly validation cycle, is a concrete design PASS can borrow or contrast with when deciding how often to retrain and recheck its own models.

Nanyang Technological University (2026). · University institutional project page

entry.title: University of Waterloo discontinues its Performance+ learning analytics dashboard pilot (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of Waterloo's Teaching Innovation Incubator reports that after instructors and staff piloted the Performance+ learning analytics dashboard in LEARN courses for two years, its EdTech Steering Committee decided not to continue licensing it. The page cites persistent challenges including difficulty navigating the interface, limited dashboard customisation, a steep learning curve for advanced features, constrained export options, and dependence on the completeness of course level LEARN data, identified through a usage review, focus groups and consultation with learning analytics practitioners; the university will instead build a coordinated, campus wide learning analytics strategy that reviews data governance and retention practices.

Why it matters here: This is a direct cautionary benchmark for PASS: a well resourced institution piloted a licensed predictive dashboard for two years and still discontinued it, not for inaccurate predictions but for interface and data quality problems and unclear governance, exactly the kind of adoption risk PASS should plan against when co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services. It argues for involving end users and reviewing data governance early, before committing to a platform, rather than after a multi-year pilot.

University of Waterloo (2025, November 3). · University institutional news page

entry.title: A fantasy-sports-style points league lifts participation in a 1,400-student engineering mechanics course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
The University of Alberta's Folio news site reports that doctoral student and teaching assistant Ahmed Mowafy Saad created the Fantasy Mechanics League, a Fantasy Premier League-style gamified teaching model used in the first-year Engineering Mechanics course (ENGG 130), which enrols up to 1,400 students across five sections of 300. Students earn points, not tied to grades, for quizzes, contests and taking turns leading problem-solving sessions as the professor. Class participation reportedly rose from about 3.5 percent to more than 25 percent, and to 56 percent once an online option was added, over two years of use reported in a Journal of ASEE study.

Why it matters here: The scale of the case (1,400 students, assessment activities that are not tied to grades) offers the Wits CheMet project a tested model for raising engagement and participation through gamified, ungraded assessment in a large first-year engineering class, a contrast and a possible point-based mechanic to adapt for crystallography and phase-transformation sessions.

McMaster, G. (2025). University of Alberta Folio. · University news report, citing a peer-reviewed ASEE study

entry.title: TU Darmstadt's browser-based serious game teaches shape memory alloys to prospective materials science students (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Technische Universität Darmstadt published Mission Metal Memory on 28 January 2025, the first title in its TUDa Campus Quest series, a browser-based 360-degree serious game that lets prospective students explore a virtual replica of the campus, attend a short lecture on shape memory alloys, work through a virtual lab and complete an interactive quiz in the Materials Science Learning Center. It was built jointly by the Institute of Materials Science, which designed the content, and the e-learning working group of the University Didactics Office, which handled the didactic design and technical implementation, within the Future Learning Spaces (FueLS) project. The page states that further games on mechanical engineering, civil engineering and architecture are in development, but it reports no player numbers or evaluation data.

Why it matters here: Shape memory alloys are a phase-transformation topic close to the CheMet project's own crystallography and phase-transformation content, and the joint content-expert-plus-instructional-designer production model is a template the Wits team could borrow for co-designing its own digital game.

Technische Universität Darmstadt (2025). · University institutional news page

entry.title: A chemistry board game paired with a custom AI chatbot lifts equilibrium test scores for pre-university students in Malaysia (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A chemistry board game called DAPoEff, developed by a team at Kolej Matrikulasi Labuan (Malaysia) and integrated with a custom AI chatbot, targets chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's Principle for pre-university and college-level chemistry students. Using the ADDIE model and a sample of 70 students across three classes, the paper reports an overall mean test score rising from 5.58 before the game to 8.02 after it, an average improvement of 2.44, with individual class gains of 2.50, 2.34 and 2.47. Student feedback, drawn from interviews and worksheets, described the game as improving understanding of equilibrium shifts and making revision more engaging.

Why it matters here: Chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's Principle call on the same reasoning students need for phase diagrams and phase transformations in metallurgy, and this project's pre-test and post-test design paired with a custom AI chatbot gives the Wits CheMet team both a measurable evaluation method and a concrete example of AI-mediated gamified learning to consider trialling alongside its own board games and digital games.

Harun, H.F. et al. (2025). Inventopia FBM-Seremban proceedings. · Innovation-competition proceedings chapter, Malaysian Ministry of Education matriculation college

entry.title: Machine learning model predicts postgraduate student engagement from enrolment data (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers from Australian Catholic University, the University of New England, Western Sydney University and Charles Darwin University built a machine learning model that scores personal, academic, intellectual, social and professional engagement from general enrolment information such as age, country of origin, prior education and time in Australia. Tested on a survey of 96 international postgraduate students at an interstate university campus, the best of eight classifiers reached accuracy of up to 85 percent and correctly flagged at-risk students up to 17 times out of 20, while also over-flagging some students who appeared well engaged.

Why it matters here: This shows a validated method, built mostly from administrative enrolment variables rather than academic records, for scoring disengagement risk in a small postgraduate cohort, a design PASS could test against the Wits School of Education's own enrolment data before full academic records are available. The authors' own caution that a different sample would likely change results is a useful reminder for PASS to validate its models across cohorts before trusting any single accuracy figure.

Shafiabady, N., Koo, T., Ud Din, F., Sattarshetty, K., Yen, M., Alazab, M., & Alsharaydeh, E. (2025). IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence. · Peer-reviewed journal article, IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence

entry.title: Gamified logistics simulation lifts accuracy and motivation in an Indonesian engineering course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universitas Telkom tested a gamified transportation and logistics simulation with 24 undergraduate Logistics Engineering students, scoring performance by the gap between a student's manual calculation and the optimal algorithmic solution. Using a pre-test and post-test design, they found a significant improvement in problem-solving accuracy and intrinsic motivation (p < 0.001), though the study had no control group and a small sample.

Why it matters here: The penalty-based scoring idea, marking students down for the distance between their answer and the correct one rather than simply right or wrong, is a concrete assessment mechanic the CheMet team could trial alongside its own board and digital games for crystallography and phase-transformation problems.

Albana, A. S., Rachmaniar, D. N. & Hajar, G. (2026). Jurnal Inovasi Teknologi Pendidikan. · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Why four machine-learning models barely beat chance at sorting at-risk learners (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher at Pangasinan State University in the Philippines, working with UNITAR International University in Malaysia, tested Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Artificial Neural Network and XGBoost models on an online learning behaviour dataset sorting students into three risk categories. Support Vector Machine scored highest at 0.40 accuracy, followed by Random Forest at 0.38, XGBoost at 0.35 and the neural network at 0.32, only modestly above the roughly 0.33 expected by chance across three categories. The author concludes the models are exploratory decision-support tools, not classifiers ready for deployment, and calls for verified institutional datasets and stronger validation before any practical use.

Why it matters here: PASS must be judged against a baseline, not just a plausible-looking score; this cautionary result is a direct check on how PASS should report and interpret its own model accuracy, and a reminder to validate against real institutional data before any early-warning flag reaches an advisor.

Dellosa, International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A small Central Asian KA171 exchange moves one student and one doctoral researcher each way (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Under a 2019 cooperation memorandum, Uzbekistan State World Languages University and 1 Decembrie 1918 University of Alba Iulia in Romania have run an Erasmus+ KA171 exchange; by February 2026 the university reported that five faculty members and four students had taken part. In one recent round a doctoral researcher spent a month at the Uzbek university studying American literature and running seminars for students and staff, while a third-year Foreign Languages and Literature student travelled to Alba Iulia for a semester.

Why it matters here: A small, low-cost KA171 exchange outside Africa (a handful of people moving each way over several years) gives the Wits-Aix-Marseille project a realistic scale comparison for its own first cohorts of students, doctoral candidates and staff.

Uzbekistan State World Languages University (2026) · University news report

entry.title: Eleven algorithms, 808 students: a small-cohort early-warning test in Nepal (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A research-grant report at Durgalaxmi Multiple Campus, Far Western University, tested eleven machine-learning and deep-learning algorithms on 808 student records across six undergraduate programmes (BA, BEd, BBA, BBS, CSIT, BSc), split 80:20 for training and testing. Random Forest performed best, reaching 82.72% accuracy, an F1-score of 86.67% and an AUC-ROC of 90.89%, narrowly ahead of XGBoost and Decision Tree, while deep-learning models underperformed on the small dataset. First-semester GPA and the number of backlog subjects were the strongest predictors of dropout.

Why it matters here: This is a realistic comparison for PASS's own early phase: a small, resource-limited institution gets strong results from Random Forest on ordinary records, while complex deep-learning models need more data than most universities, including Wits, are likely to have ready at the outset.

Ojha, Far Western University research-grant report, 2026 · Institutional research-grant report, examined by the university's Research Management Committee

entry.title: Cairo University and a Bulgarian business school open a KA171 exchange for commerce and tourism students (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Cairo University's International Relations Office opened an Erasmus+ KA171 exchange with the International Business School in Bulgaria for undergraduate, master's and PhD students in administration and management, economics, and tourism, for one semester in Spring 2026; master's students could also apply for a two-month mobility. The notice set a deadline of 18 December 2025 and required a learning agreement, proof of English at B2 level, a one-page motivation letter and a two-page CV, warning that incomplete or late applications would be discarded.

Why it matters here: A live example of the KA171 mechanism that the Wits-Aix-Marseille project itself relies on, setting out exactly the fields, eligibility rules and paperwork candidates must meet, and a useful benchmark for the deadlines and documents the Wits-Aix-Marseille call will need to set.

Cairo University International Relations Office (2025) · University International Relations Office notice

entry.title: A student-led 'Game Day' for chemical engineering wellbeing, reflected on as a seven-step model (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
The Chemical Engineering Student Association at a South African university piloted a discipline-based recreational 'Game Day' in 2022, offering undergraduates a relaxed space for games, peer connection and relief from academic pressure. A 2025 qualitative case study by two South African academics, built on reflections from current and former student representatives, proposes a seven-step action-research framework so other departments can adapt the idea, while noting it relied on informal feedback rather than formal outcome measures.

Why it matters here: It is a reminder that games in engineering education do not have to teach content to matter: a low-cost, student-run Game Day alongside the CheMet study's own teaching games could support the wellbeing and sense of community that make students more receptive to learning in the first place.

Roopchund, R. & Seedat, N. (2025). Scholarship of Teaching and Learning in the South. · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Randomised trial finds an escape room beats a lecture for teaching software engineering (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid randomly assigned 326 second-year software engineering students to learn software modelling either through a virtual educational escape room (164 students) or a traditional lecture (162 students). The escape room group reported very positive perceptions of the activity and significantly outperformed the lecture group on a knowledge test, while the authors note the trial covered a single course and institution.

Why it matters here: A randomised design with over 300 students is far larger evidence than most gamification studies the group has reviewed, and it is a useful benchmark for how the CheMet team might eventually test whether its own board and digital games outperform conventional teaching, not just whether students enjoy them.

Gordillo, A. & López-Fernández, D. (2024). IEEE Transactions on Education. · Peer-reviewed journal article (IEEE Transactions on Education)

entry.title: A Kenyan-built early alert tool tested on 21,000 Open University learners (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A master's thesis at Strathmore University's Institute of Mathematical Sciences in Nairobi compared Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machine on 21,216 records from the UK's Open University, then built a performance-prediction and early-alert tool in R-Shiny. Logistic Regression performed best, with a precision rate of 90%; demographic information and academic history were the strongest features.

Why it matters here: The study shows a lean, open-source early-alert tool is within reach for a team outside the big data-science hubs, using an openly available dataset; it is a concrete build pattern PASS could trial once its own anonymised Wits data is ready, before scaling to richer institutional variables.

Ng'eno, Strathmore University master's thesis, 2024 · Master's thesis, institutional repository

entry.title: An Erasmus+ multilingualism course for teachers, built by eight universities in seven countries (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Teacher Education About Multilingualism (TEAM) was an Erasmus+ Strategic Partnership (September 2020 to August 2023) among eight universities in seven countries, led by Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań and including the University of Edinburgh, the University of Granada and Bar-Ilan University, working through the Bilingualism Matters network. It produced a free, open, login-free online course on bilingualism research for pre-service and in-service teachers, plus a set of educational videos on why multilingualism matters to teachers and what affects multilingual development; the course was recognised by Poland's Erasmus+ national agency as an example of good practice.

Why it matters here: A ready-made, free multilingual-teacher-training course built by a seven-country Erasmus+ partnership, giving the Wits-Aix-Marseille project's master's students in bilingual teaching a tested model and open resource to adapt rather than build from nothing.

Bilingualism Matters network (2023) · Project partner's own network page

entry.title: A Finnish scholar warns that AI tools in virtual exchange can smooth away the friction that teaches intercultural communication (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A 2026 perspective article by Judit Háhn of the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, published in Frontiers in Computer Science, argues that AI translation, captioning and generative tools can lower language barriers and spread communicative responsibility more evenly in virtual exchange, drawing on an example of students using generative AI image and translation tools to build multilingual, multimodal meaning. It warns, citing Hackett and Dawson (2026), that the same tools can reduce the linguistic negotiation and repair work that underpins intercultural learning, a 'paradox of communicative friction' in which smoothing communication can weaken the interactional conditions for relational learning. It recommends making AI mediation visible, prioritising dialogue over task completion, and treating learners' full linguistic répertoires as legitimate resources, rather than removing all friction.

Why it matters here: This is a direct caution for any AI-supported language or virtual mobility tool the Erasmus+/CIVIS exchange adopts for students who cannot travel: it argues that removing every communicative difficulty with translation AI can quietly remove the very negotiation work that bilingual and multilingual teacher education is meant to build, so any blended mobility design should decide deliberately which friction to keep.

Háhn, Frontiers in Computer Science, 8 (2026) · Peer-reviewed perspective article, Frontiers in Computer Science, open access, confirmed by fetching the article page directly.

entry.title: A Mexico City gathering sets out the scale of Erasmus+ mobility between Latin America, the Caribbean and Europe (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The European Commission's education departments, the EU Delegation to Mexico and ANUIES held the Regional Erasmus+ Week 2026 in Mexico City on 6 to 8 October 2026, bringing together Erasmus+ project participants and about 30 national focal points from Latin America, the Caribbean and Europe. The announcement states that the 2025 selection round alone created almost 1,300 mobility partnerships between European and Latin American or Caribbean universities, with close to 8,000 students and staff planned to travel to Europe and more than 3,500 Europeans travelling the other way, alongside 76 higher-education and 31 vocational capacity-building projects, within a 2021 to 2027 Erasmus+ budget for the two regions exceeding 152 million euros.

Why it matters here: The scale given here, almost 1,300 university-to-university partnerships funded through the same KA171 mobility strand that underpins the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange, shows how far a single Erasmus+ corridor can grow, and is a useful benchmark and potential partner network (ANUIES, the EU Delegation to Mexico) should the Wits AHEAD group ever look to extend bilingual teacher education mobility beyond its Africa-Europe partnership into Latin America.

EU Delegation to Mexico, press release, 30 September 2026 · Official European Union délégation press release, confirmed by fetching the page directly.

entry.title: A Portuguese polytechnic designs an AI dashboard that explains why a student is at risk (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A 2026 short paper from the Polytechnic of Porto describes Ogma, a learning analytics platform that combines student coursework, grade records, forum messages and other educational application logs into a dynamic risk profile for each student. Instructors see a dashboard with graded alerts, plain-language explanations of the main risk factors, and recovery recommendations generated by a pipeline that mixes machine learning, retrieval-augmented generation and large language models. The paper is a design and architecture study; no pilot results or accuracy figures are yet reported.

Why it matters here: Ogma's emphasis on explaining each alert, rather than issuing a bare risk score, is a direct answer to the trust problem PASS must solve before Wits advisors act on a predictive flag, and its reference architecture is worth testing against the anonymised Wits School of Education data PASS already holds.

Queiros, 7th International Computer Programming Education Conference (ICPEC 2026) · Peer-reviewed conference short paper, Open Access Series in Informatics (OASIcs), confirmed by fetching the Dagstuhl record directly.

entry.title: A computer-based crystallography game outperforms its virtual-reality predecessor for engineering materials students (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign built Crystal Vision, a virtual-reality game that let 84 undergraduate civil engineering students explore 3D crystallographic structures for the course CEE 300: Behavior of Materials; it produced strong engagement but was limited by motion sickness, discomfort and hardware needs. A computer-based sequel, Crystal Vision 2.0, was then tested with 82 undergraduate students and produced a 9% higher post-game conceptual quiz score and a 10% shorter quiz completion time than the VR version, while needing no specialised headset.

Why it matters here: For CheMet, this is direct evidence that a lightweight, browser- or desktop-based crystallography game can teach 3D structure concepts at least as well as a costlier VR version, a practical model to borrow for teaching crystal systems and phase diagrams without needing a VR headset for every student.

Tabassum, Amos, Henschen, Shaffer and Garg, 2026 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper (work in progress), American Society for Engineering Education, confirmed by fetching the paper PDF directly (identical copy also verified via the paper's DOI).

entry.title: A Bangladeshi university team builds an explainable model of what actually moves a student's CGPA (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A 2025 study from Jahangirnagar University in Dhaka, Bangladesh, surveyed 1,050 university students and built models of the socio-academic and economic factors behind their CGPA, using Ridge Regression for prediction and Random Forest for classifying performance levels, explained with SHAP, LIME and Interpret. The Random Forest classifier reached 98.68 per cent accuracy, and the explanations pointed to study hours, scholarships, parental education and prior academic performance as the strongest factors. The authors built a web application to give students personalised feedback from the model.

Why it matters here: The explainable-AI toolkit (SHAP, LIME) and the choice of everyday, collectable factors such as study hours and scholarship status give PASS a tested method for making a Wits predictive model's reasoning visible to students and advisors, not just its score.

Akter, Hosen, Ahmed, Anannya and Hossain, arXiv preprint, 2025 · arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, confirmed by fetching the paper's full text directly.

entry.title: A marble-based board game teaches engineering students materials selection through Ashby charts (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Engineers at the University of Victoria, with collaborators at California Polytechnic State University and ANSYS Inc. in the United States, built the Multi-Material Marbles Game, in which students measure mechanical loss coefficient, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity and mass density on spherical marbles made from different material families and plot the results on a Material Property Chart, or Ashby plot. Aimed at high-school seniors and first-year engineering students, pilot studies with the open-source game found high engagement and increased interest in materials science; all its CAD designs, instructions and material cards are published openly for other instructors to reuse.

Why it matters here: This is a ready-made, open-source hands-on format for teaching materials selection and property comparison, a tactile alternative CheMet could trial alongside its digital gamified assessments, and the published CAD and card files mean Wits could adapt the marbles directly to teach crystallography or phase-transformation properties.

Barnsdale, Daugela, Galos, Hulse, Tyler and Yu, 2025 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education, confirmed by fetching the paper PDF directly.

entry.title: ASEAN sets out conditions for teacher mobility across member states, including language proficiency (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A 2025 ASEAN Secretariat trend report on teacher professional development and mobility describes the SEAMEO SEA-Teacher programme, which has placed teacher trainees in month-long practicums in other ASEAN member states since 2016, and the Philippine Normal University's Project TEACH exchange programme. Citing Symaco (2023), it sets out six conditions for intra-ASEAN teacher mobility, including that recipient countries must recognise an applicant's qualifications, state clearly why they are hiring migrant teachers, and state language proficiency requirements where the teaching language differs from the migrant teacher's own. The report recommends short-term ASEAN teaching stints so teachers gain multicultural competence and regional language proficiency, as part of a push to recruit 4.5 million more teachers across the region by 2030.

Why it matters here: The report sets out, in one regional bloc, the practical conditions (qualification recognition, immigration policy, stated language requirements) that any Africa-Europe mobility scheme such as Erasmus+ KA171 or CIVIS must also solve, and SEA-Teacher is a working model of short, month-long reciprocal placements that the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange could borrow for staff and doctoral mobility.

ASEAN Secretariat, ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Trend Report No. 15 (2025) · Intergovernmental trend report, ASEAN Secretariat, confirmed by reading the extracted PDF text directly.

entry.title: A Panamanian university tests three models for spotting students at risk, built with a formal data-mining process (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A 2025 study at the Technological University of Panama followed the CRISP-DM data-mining methodology to build a context-aware predictive model for students at risk of dropping out, drawing on academic, socio-demographic and university-context data. The team compared Logistic Regression, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting across several scenarios; Random Forest in the third scenario gave the strongest balance of accuracy and generalisation. The authors note that limited access to real psychological data constrained how complete the model could be.

Why it matters here: UTP's disciplined CRISP-DM process, and its honesty about a missing data source limiting the model, is a useful methodological template and a cautionary note for PASS as it works out which Wits data sources are actually available before promising a complete risk picture.

Arenales, Villarreal and Saldana Barrios, Ingenieria Solidaria, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Ingenieria Solidaria (Universidad Cooperativa de Colombia), confirmed by fetching the article page directly.

entry.title: LogicHouse: a web-based serious game for teaching digital electronics across Nigerian and South African universities (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Covenant University in Nigeria, with Durban University of Technology, Mangosuthu University of Technology and Stellenbosch University in South Africa, built LogicHouse-V1, a web-based serious game in which players fix a virtual broken house by solving digital electronics problems such as logic gates and circuit design. Designed with the Learning Mechanics-Game Mechanics model and built with Unity, C# and Microsoft Azure PlayFab, then deployed free on itch.io, the game's preliminary evaluation found students interested in it and its application, with the authors reporting a prospect of improved performance in courses that use it.

Why it matters here: This is a rare Africa-led example of a serious game built specifically for a core undergraduate engineering course, evidence that a browser-playable game can be designed and evaluated across Nigerian and South African institutions with modest, freely available tools, a collaboration model CheMet could adapt for a crystallography or phase-transformation game shared between Wits and partner universities.

Ajayi, Adetiba, Ifijeh, Abayomi, Wejin, Thakur and Moyo, Cogent Engineering, 11(1), 2024 · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article (Creative Commons CC BY 4.0), Cogent Engineering, confirmed via Crossref and OpenAlex metadata and the published abstract.

entry.title: Engineering students at a Chilean university build a tower defense game to teach secondary-school chemistry (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three students on Universidad de Talca's Civil Engineering in Intelligent Systems and Video Games programme built Chemistry TD, a tower defense game in which players combine chemical elements to build defences, to teach the naming and synthesis of simple compounds set out in Chile's first and second year secondary chemistry curriculum. The team matched the game's mechanics to the curriculum's objectives and presented the work at the 44th International Conference of the Chilean Computer Science Society. Their supervisor said testing had been done but gave no results, and the students plan to trial the game in schools to measure its effect on learning.

Why it matters here: The project shows engineering students, rather than education researchers, designing a game directly around a specific curriculum's content, a useful contrast for the Wits team as it builds its own crystallography and phase-transformation games around what metallurgical engineering students are actually assessed on, and a reminder that a game's classroom impact still needs to be measured once it is built.

G5 Noticias, 17 September 2026, reporting on work from Universidad de Talca presented at the 44th International Conference of the Chilean Computer Science Society (SCCC) · Chilean news report on a university project, confirmed by fetching the article directly; the underlying work was presented at the 44th SCCC conference and is reported as later published on IEEE Xplore.

entry.title: A Jordanian university tests gamified quizzes across two internet of things engineering courses (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A 2026 study at Applied Science Private University in Amman, Jordan, tested gamified formative assessment quizzes with 75 undergraduate students across two internet of things courses, DevOps for IoT and human-computer interaction in IoT, in spring 2025. The gamified platform used visual feedback, progress indicators and interactive elements, and the two courses produced markedly different results: performance was higher in the human-computer interaction course and lower where fill-in-the-blank questions were used. The authors concluded that how well gamification works depends on matching question format and content difficulty to what students already know.

Why it matters here: The study is a caution for the CheMet project: the same gamified quiz design did not work equally well across two technical courses, which supports testing any gamified quiz on crystallography or phase transformations carefully before relying on it, and matching question format to how well students already know the material.

Shaban and Al Tawil, International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 15(3), 2249-2260 (2026) · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article, International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IAES), confirmed by fetching the article page directly.

entry.title: An Erasmus+-funded early-intervention pilot shows how slowly learning analytics spreads inside one university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of Bergen's SLATE centre, Norway's national hub for learning analytics research, reports in an EU Erasmus+ project deliverable that only two course teams agreed to pilot early intervention dashboards under the ISILA project, despite the university hosting the country's leading learning analytics researchers, and that a change of lead investigator further slowed progress. The pilots nonetheless produced two concrete design changes, letting students choose which digital activity to track and adding numerical grades to previously pass or fail assessments so they could feed dashboards, and the university has since convened a cross institutional working group focused on first year retention as it renews its learning management system.

Why it matters here: The report's frank account of how hard it was to get even two course teams to adopt early intervention dashboards, despite deep institutional expertise, is a realistic caution for the PASS team as it moves from building predictive models to persuading Wits academics and the Business Intelligence Services to actually use them in day to day advising.

Kitto and Jovanovic, ISILA project impact report, University of Bergen, 2026 · Official public deliverable of the EU Erasmus+-funded ISILA project (ref. 2023-1-FI01-KA220-HED-000159757), written by the University of Bergen's own learning analytics centre; read in full from the published report PDF.

entry.title: Comparing machine learning and deep learning for early identification of at-risk university students in Jordan (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Al-Zaytoonah University of Jordan compared three machine learning algorithms, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and XGBoost, against two deep learning models, a deep neural network and TabNet, for predicting dropout among 4,424 higher education students, then tested whether the SMOTE and Borderline-SMOTE balancing techniques improved detection of at-risk students. On the original dataset XGBoost reached the highest accuracy, 92.84 per cent, and recall, 88.03 per cent, and machine learning models consistently outperformed the deep learning models across the original and both balanced versions of the dataset. Applying Borderline-SMOTE raised recall further, at some cost to the other metrics, with XGBoost combined with Borderline-SMOTE judged the best overall approach for catching dropout cases.

Why it matters here: PASS will have to make the same two choices this study tested directly, which family of models to trust and whether to rebalance the data so fewer at-risk students are missed, so its finding that simpler machine learning models beat deep learning ones, and that balancing techniques trade some precision for better detection of true dropouts, is directly transferable evidence for how the Wits and Emory team tunes its own predictive model before it reaches advising staff.

Aljawazneh, Alqirem and Al-Adwan, Al-Zaytoonah University Journal of Business, 2026 · Peer-reviewed article in the Al-Zaytoonah University Journal of Business (Vol 2, No 1, March 2026); read in full from the published PDF, including the complete results tables for all three dataset versions.

entry.title: The European Commission's review of the European Universities initiative finds real momentum, but says alliances still need to widen their reach (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The European Commission's account of the European Universities initiative, the EU scheme of cross-border alliances that includes CIVIS, last updated in November 2025, reports progress across five dimensions: shared governance, joint education and mobility, cooperation with society and the economy, research and innovation, and wider system change. It states that the initiative's alliances now have more than 2,200 associated partners in their local and regional ecosystems, and names excellence, inclusivity and geographical balance as its clearest strengths so far. The Commission adds that reach still needs to widen to more students, staff and faculty, with further coordinated European and national policy action still needed.

Why it matters here: CIVIS, the alliance that already links Aix-Marseille and Wits, sits inside this wider picture, so the Commission's finding that alliances still need to widen their reach to staff and students is a reminder to build the new KA171 mobility between Johannesburg and Marseille to include administrative staff and early-career candidates from the outset, not only the most mobile few.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture, European Education Area, 2025 · Official European Commission page for the European Universities initiative, part of the European Education Area website; fetched and read directly.

entry.title: A Malaysian chemical engineering lecturer builds a board game for a stalled petroleum refining course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A 2025 study at Universiti Teknologi MARA in Shah Alam, Malaysia, introduced a board game built for a final-semester petroleum refining engineering course, where motivation on complex, interdependent topics had been flagging. Across two groups totalling 52 students, exit surveys found 92 to 100 per cent of students rated learning, organisation, teamwork, instructor support and topic coverage positively, with 88.5 per cent satisfied with the workload. The author frames the game as a motivational, application-focused complement to direct instruction, not a replacement, and calls for future work to pair this satisfaction data with direct measures of learning.

Why it matters here: The high but purely self-reported satisfaction scores are a direct parallel for the Wits study's own classroom observation and interview plans: a reminder to check, through tests or observation, whether students' grasp of phase transformations or structure-property relationships actually improved, rather than relying on how much they say they enjoyed the game.

Majnis, International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science, 9(24), 491-496 (2025) · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article, International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science, confirmed by fetching the article page directly.

entry.title: An open, anonymised dataset of 39,000 students' trajectories for dropout and retention research (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A ten-member team at the Universitat Politècnica de València, a Spanish technological university, has published a fully anonymised dataset covering 39,364 students, 4,989 courses and 163 degree programmes across three academic years, excluding pandemic-affected periods. Its 464,739 records, one per student per course enrolment, combine admission pathway, academic performance, socio-demographic and socioeconomic characteristics with learning management system digital engagement and Wi-Fi access patterns, and the dataset is released under a CC BY 4.0 licence explicitly for research on academic performance, retention, dropout and predictive modelling of at-risk students.

Why it matters here: PASS is starting with anonymised data from one School and will need to decide which variables beyond grades genuinely predict risk, so this dataset's combination of digital engagement and access pattern data alongside conventional academic and socioeconomic variables, released openly at this scale, is a model the Wits and Emory team could trial or benchmark its own model against as it expands beyond its first dataset.

Igualde-Sáez et al., Universitat Politècnica de València, Zenodo, 2025 · Open research dataset published on Zenodo under a CC BY 4.0 licence by a ten-member university team; read in full from the dataset's own description page, which the team maintains directly.

entry.title: A University World News essay reframes Africa's academic brain drain as an institutional accounting failure, and proposes split appointments (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Writing for University World News, reposted by the University of Cape Town's Second-Order University platform, the commentator K Kefale argues that treating African academics' emigration as ordinary migration hides an institutional failure. Publicly funded training, the essay says, too often becomes a transfer of value to institutions abroad, a process it calls decapitalisation, caused by low pay, weak infrastructure, political interference in appointments, visa regimes and funding models that reward working overseas. The essay sets out a reform package built around split appointments, with a primary post kept in Africa, defined time each year in a partner laboratory abroad, joint doctoral committees as the default, and a rule that grant spending and doctoral supervision mostly stay with the African institution.

Why it matters here: For a scheme moving staff and doctoral candidates between Johannesburg and Marseille, this essay is a direct challenge to design the exchange as circulation rather than departure: its call for joint doctoral committees, co-supervision by default, and spending that stays mostly with the African partner is close to what the KA171 agreement could build in from the start.

Kefale, K., University World News, republished by the University of Cape Town, 2025 · Opinion essay by an academic commentator, first published by University World News and republished by the University of Cape Town's Second-Order University platform; fetched and read directly in full.

entry.title: CIVIS runs a coordinated Erasmus+ route for staff and doctoral mobility between its European members and six African partner universities (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European Civic University Alliance that includes Aix-Marseille Université, runs a coordinated call that lets academics, postdoctoral researchers, PhD candidates and administrative staff move in either direction between its European members and six partner universities in Africa, among them the University of the Witwatersrand. The scheme is funded through Erasmus+ International Credit Mobility (KA171), pays travel and subsistence at the usual ICM rates with extra support for participants with fewer opportunities, and sets stays of five days to two months for staff and up to six months for PhD candidates. Applicants must find their own host and apply directly through the KA171 office at both universities, since CIVIS states that it cannot help arrange a host.

Why it matters here: Wits is one of the six African partner universities named in this CIVIS call, and Aix-Marseille is both the lead of the new Wits-AMU KA171-HED project and a CIVIS member, so this coordinated route is a live, parallel channel the new partnership can point staff and doctoral candidates towards, or use as a model for its own application paperwork.

CIVIS (European Civic University Alliance), via the Fundit funding portal, 2023, updated 2026 · CIVIS alliance's own official coordinated call, hosted on the Fundit European funding portal; fetched and read directly, including the page's structured metadata confirming original publication on 15 December 2023 and a page update on 23 April 2026.

entry.title: Fixing one group's fairness score for a vendor's early-warning system can simply shift the unfairness onto another group (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Toronto and the Georgia Institute of Technology rebuilt a vendor-style early-warning model using 168,550 first-semester records from a publicly funded Ontario college, because the real vendor system could not be inspected. Before any correction, the model predicted success for 85.6 per cent of international students against 70.4 per cent of domestic students, and testing six post-hoc fairness methods found none closed this gap without creating a new one elsewhere: one method raised false positive rates for female students from 56.1 to 83.7 per cent, hiding genuinely struggling students from advisors, while another flagged roughly half of all students, far beyond what advisers could act on.

Why it matters here: The PASS project is built on predictive models that will flag Wits students for advising support, so this study's warning that institutions buying off-the-shelf early-warning systems cannot simply bolt on a fairness fix without checking what it does elsewhere in the model is a direct caution for how PASS's own interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services should be audited before, not after, they go live.

McConvey, Zhai, Li and Guha, arXiv preprint, 2026 · Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed), arXiv, posted 29 September 2026; read in full via the arXiv HTML version, with data, methods and results fully reported.

entry.title: A Colombian university adds AI-generated synthetic data to sharpen dropout-risk prediction for its rarest at-risk cases (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universidad del Cauca built a hybrid dropout-prediction model that adds synthetic data, generated with business rules and statistically validated, to the training set alongside real student records, while keeping evaluation on untouched real data to avoid leakage. The approach specifically targets the smallest and hardest-to-predict group, students who do drop out, and the authors report that adding synthetic cases to training improved precision, recall and F1-score for that minority class. The method sits within the CRISP-DM data-mining framework and was presented at the DATA 2026 conference in Porto.

Why it matters here: PASS is starting from a relatively small, anonymised Wits School of Education dataset in which actual dropout cases will be rare, so this Colombian group's method for safely enlarging the minority class with validated synthetic data, without touching the real test set, is a concrete technique the project could trial once its own predictive models are built.

Caicedo, Muñoz and Diaz, Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Data Science, Technology and Applications (DATA), 2026 · Peer-reviewed conference paper, DATA 2026 proceedings (SciTePress), confirmed via DOI resolution and the publisher's abstract.

entry.title: A Thai secondary-school engineering game clears its own 80 per cent efficiency bar (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers built a board game called 'Zero Carbon' to teach engineering design skills and environmental awareness, and tested it with 36 eleventh-grade students at a Thai school chosen by stratified random sampling. The game met its own efficiency criteria (E1/E2 of 80.93/83.05), and students' post-game scores on engineering design skills and environmental awareness were significantly above an 80 per cent benchmark.

Why it matters here: The game's efficiency-and-effectiveness testing method, checking a game against a numerical benchmark before trusting its learning claims, gives the Wits project a simple, replicable yardstick to apply to its own board and digital games for crystallography and phase transformations.

Ekwaraphaisankul and Klaisuwan, Srinakharinwirot University Engineering Journal, 2026 · Peer-reviewed article, Srinakharinwirot University Engineering Journal, confirmed by fetching the published article page.

entry.title: Seventy-five Indian students begin fully funded Erasmus Mundus master's degrees, backed by a new student ambassadors' network (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The European Union's Delegation to India held a send-off for 75 Indian students awarded two-year Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's Degree scholarships for 2026 to 2028, to study at universities across 15 European countries in fields including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, renewable energy and pharmaceutical sciences. India has been the largest single beneficiary of Erasmus Mundus scholarships since the programme began in 2004. At the same event the European Union launched an EU-India Student Ambassadors' Network of 40 students from 20 universities across 14 Indian states and union territories.

Why it matters here: India's position as the single largest beneficiary of Erasmus Mundus is a useful point of contrast for the much smaller, bilateral Wits-Aix-Marseille KA171 exchange, and the Student Ambassadors' Network is a ready-made model the project's own administrative staff could adapt to keep past mobility participants connected to new candidates.

European Union Delegation to India, reported by Devdiscourse, 2026 · News report of an EU Delegation to India ceremony; the EU Delegation's own page could not be fetched directly (bot-protected), so this is confirmed against the Devdiscourse report, consistent with other outlets covering the same event.

entry.title: A 33-million-article bibliometric study maps where the world's researchers are gained and lost (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Three researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research traced changes in author affiliations across more than 33 million journal articles and 19 million authors to build annual sequences of internal and international researcher migration for 1,941 subnational regions in 211 countries and territories between 2005 and 2020. They identify five distinct migration trajectories and find that gains and losses of researchers often sit side by side within the same country, including in major scientific hubs. OECD membership, research and development spending, and population size were the strongest correlates of a region's trajectory.

Why it matters here: This bibliometric method of tracking where academics move to and from at a fine-grained regional level offers the KA171 project a model for eventually measuring its own mobility's effect on researcher retention at Wits and at Aix-Marseille, rather than simply counting how many staff and students took part.

Slocombe, Rowe and Akbaritabar, MPIDR Working Paper, 2026 · Open-access working paper, Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research, confirmed by fetching the publisher's own abstract page.

entry.title: A Nigerian forecasting study finds Europe's grip on African student mobility is loosening (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Two Nigerian researchers used statistical, deep learning and ensemble forecasting models to study historical patterns in African tertiary student mobility across eight world regions. North America and Western Europe remain Africa's main historical destinations, but East Asia and the Pacific, and the Arab States, are drawing growing numbers of African students. The study also finds rising mobility within Sub-Saharan Africa itself, suggesting more academic collaboration between African countries.

Why it matters here: For a partnership moving staff and students in both directions between Johannesburg and Marseille, this is a reminder that Europe can no longer assume Africa's outbound student mobility: African universities and students increasingly have other regions to choose from, which strengthens the case for the KA171 exchange to stay genuinely reciprocal rather than one-way.

Shikaa and Igiri, Journal of International Students, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Journal of International Students, confirmed via DOI resolution and the publisher's abstract page.

entry.title: A Taiwanese early-warning system pairs algorithmic risk scores with culturally adapted mentoring, and most flagged students go on to pass (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Taiwan's National University of Tainan and National Formosa University built an early-warning system from learning-management-system data for 2,856 students across 64 courses, finding that past grades, attendance and assignment submission were the strongest predictors of risk, with the model reaching a balanced accuracy (AUC) of 0.85. In a quasi-experimental trial, 48 students flagged as at risk received a personalised intervention designed around Confucian educational values rather than a generic alert, and 73 per cent of them went on to pass, a large improvement (Cohen's d = 0.91) over students who received no such support.

Why it matters here: PASS is explicitly built to pair predictive flags with co-created interventions through the University's Business Intelligence Services rather than stopping at the score, and this is a rare published example of that full prediction-to-intervention cycle measured end to end: evidence that a culturally adapted follow-up, not the algorithm alone, is what moved outcomes.

Chang, Chen and Lee, Education Sciences, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Education Sciences (MDPI), open access, confirmed via Crossref metadata.

entry.title: A Colombian serious game turns production-process optimisation into a team assessment (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
An industrial engineering lecturer at Medellín's Instituto Tecnológico Metropolitano designed a serious game that asks student teams to identify, formulate and solve a complex production-process optimisation problem, aligning the game directly with the course's own learning outcomes. Comparing each team's net-utility result against the optimal solution from formal optimisation techniques, the study found the game strengthened achievement of the stated learning outcomes and rated well on usability and player experience in a perception survey.

Why it matters here: Its method, designing a game's mechanics and scoring to match specific, pre-stated learning outcomes and then checking results against a known correct answer, offers the Wits project a disciplined template for using games as assessment rather than only as practice, directly relevant to the diversified assessment strand of the metallurgical engineering study.

Hernández, Ingeniería y Competitividad, 2025 · Peer-reviewed original article, Ingeniería y Competitividad, open access, confirmed via DOI resolution and the full text PDF.

entry.title: A Mozambican university trials game design elements in Moodle to raise student engagement (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A 2025 master's thesis at the University of Cape Town followed three lecturers and 112 students at Mozambique's Eduardo Mondlane University as they used points, levels, leaderboards and immediate feedback inside the Moodle learning management system. Interviews and student questionnaires, analysed with QualCoder and SPSS, found the gamified design supported the teacher's own teaching cycle and raised both lecturers' and students' satisfaction with Moodle and their intention to keep using it.

Why it matters here: The study offers the Wits project a worked case of adding game elements to an existing learning management system rather than building a stand-alone game, and its mixed teacher-interview and student-questionnaire design is close to the surveys, interviews and classroom observation already planned for the metallurgical engineering study.

Tivane, University of Cape Town, 2025 · Master's thesis (MEd), University of Cape Town institutional repository (OpenUCT), confirmed by fetching the thesis record directly.

entry.title: Logistic regression and random forest both reach above 90 per cent accuracy in a Lithuanian dropout study (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher at Vilnius Gediminas Technical University compared six machine-learning models, logistic regression, support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, k-nearest neighbours and a neural network, on an open-access dataset of 4,424 student records with 36 attributes. Logistic regression and random forest performed best, reaching accuracy above 90 per cent and a ROC AUC of up to 0.96, with first and second semester academic performance, tuition fee payment status, outstanding debt, scholarship status, age at enrolment and study programme the most significant risk factors.

Why it matters here: The study's comparison of simple, interpretable models such as logistic regression against more complex ones, on routinely collected enrolment and fee data rather than bespoke instruments, gives PASS a benchmark for how far an interpretable baseline model can go before the Wits-Emory team turns to more complex methods, and its risk-factor list (fees, scholarships, age at enrolment) is a useful checklist against the Business Intelligence Services data.

Mincevičius, New Trends in Computer Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access, confirmed via DOI resolution and the publisher's own article page.

entry.title: An opinion piece argues Belgium's tighter student visa rules fall heaviest on African applicants (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
An opinion piece in The Brussels Times argues that Belgium's tightened rules for non-EU students, which require bachelor's students to accumulate 100 credits by the end of their third year, raise the required proof of funds to 1,050 euro a month and allow fees of up to 17,500 euro a year at some institutions, filter students by wealth rather than merit. It reports more than 2,615 student visa rejections in the preceding cycle, falling heavily on applicants from Cameroon and Morocco, and calls for Belgium to replace brain-drain fears with a brain-circulation model of trade-aligned visa pathways, diaspora scholarships and post-study search years.

Why it matters here: As a mobility scheme that depends on African partner universities and on African students and staff being able to obtain visas, the Wits and Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ project has a direct stake in this kind of evidence on how tightening student visa rules can disproportionately affect African applicants elsewhere in Europe, and in the brain-circulation alternative the piece proposes.

Nweke, The Brussels Times, 2026 · Opinion article in an established Belgian English-language news outlet, confirmed by fetching the page.

entry.title: An enterprise system switch gives a Caribbean campus one-click visibility into which students have stopped returning (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The University of the West Indies Five Islands Campus in Antigua moved to an Ellucian Banner enterprise system in July 2025, covering student registration, finance, accounts receivable, data migration and reporting and analytics. Campus Registrar Dr Camille Samuel reported that the platform gives her team one-click visibility into student progress and retention, letting staff identify students who have not returned and intervene early.

Why it matters here: This is a small Caribbean campus choosing an off-the-shelf enterprise system, rather than a bespoke model, to get early-alert visibility, which is a relevant contrast for PASS as the Wits-Emory team weighs a purpose-built predictive model against the reporting tools the University's Business Intelligence Services already runs.

Antigua News, 2026 · News report, Antigua News, confirmed by fetching the published article.

entry.title: Two Tanzanian teacher educators complete a staff mobility placement at a Finnish university (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Two teacher educators from the Dar es Salaam University College of Education in Tanzania spent a two-week staff mobility placement at the University of Eastern Finland from 13 to 27 March 2026, hosted jointly with the Finnish National Agency for Education. The visit, held under the Future Teachers in East Africa (FUTE) project, included teaching, school visits and joint curriculum work, and continued a longer-term partnership on teacher education between the two institutions.

Why it matters here: A short, reciprocal staff placement built around joint curriculum work and school visits, rather than a one-off conference trip, offers a concrete format for the shorter staff exchanges envisaged under the Wits and Aix-Marseille Erasmus+ project, and the sustained Finland-Tanzania partnership behind it is a further point of comparison for how the Wits School of Education and Aix-Marseille's INSPE might deepen their own exchange over successive mobility rounds.

University of Eastern Finland, School of Applied Educational Science and Teacher Education, 2026 · Institutional news item, University of Eastern Finland, confirmed by fetching the page.

entry.title: A neural network outperforms eight other models in predicting dropout at Côte d'Ivoire's virtual university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Virtual University of Côte d'Ivoire compared nine machine-learning and deep-learning models on 9,881 student records with 14 features. A neural network performed best, with an F1 score of 0.9888 and accuracy of 0.9930, ahead of gradient boosting, the best traditional machine-learning model, at an F1 score of 0.9406 and accuracy of 0.9641.

Why it matters here: A fully online, Francophone West African university reaching this scale of comparison, nine models on nearly 10,000 records, shows PASS what a resource-constrained, fully digital institution can build from its own enrolment data, and the gap between the neural network and the simpler gradient-boosting model is a useful caution for the Wits-Emory team on how much complexity the Business Intelligence Services data can justify.

Kone and Achi, International Journal of Advanced Research, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Advanced Research), confirmed via DOI resolution to the publisher's page and cross-checked against the authors' Zenodo deposit of the same study.

entry.title: A mixed-methods study measures gains from Kahoot-based gamification in aircraft maintenance training (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A study at the Philippine State College of Aeronautics assessed 120 participants in Aircraft Maintenance Technology education using Kahoot-based gamification, combining quantitative surveys, pre- and post-assessments and qualitative interviews with students and instructors. The study reports statistically significant gains after the gamified intervention: engagement up by 43.8 per cent, motivation by 55.2 per cent, knowledge retention by 41.2 per cent and practical skills by 51.6 per cent. It also names internet connectivity, time constraints and question-format limitations as practical challenges, and recommends blending gamification with hands-on training and technologies such as augmented and virtual reality.

Why it matters here: The size of the measured gains across engagement, retention and practical skills gives the Wits project a concrete benchmark for what a well-run Kahoot-style quiz layer can add on top of hands-on technical training, and its identified barriers, connectivity, time and question format, are exactly the practical constraints the co-design workshops with metallurgical engineering students will need to plan around.

Dela Peña, Research in Learning Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Research in Learning Technology (Association for Learning Technology), open access, confirmed via DOI resolution.
